chief_complaint: fatigue, hyperpigmentation of skin, and orthostatic hypotension
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with fatigue, hyperpigmentation of skin, and orthostatic hypotension. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his darkened skin and constant dizziness are just severe dehydration and chronic exhaustion from working outdoors in the sun.
concerns: He is worried that he might faint while driving his children to school or collapse suddenly on a job site.
expectations: He hopes to receive IV fluids or a prescription today to stop the dizzy spells and keep his blood pressure steady.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Addison Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes starting oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone and checking baseline cortisol for Addison Disease, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: fatigue, hyperpigmentation of skin, and orthostatic hypotension

Key HPI features: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with fatigue, hyperpigmentation of skin, and orthostatic hypotension. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Addison Disease.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Addison Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Anemia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs of impending adrenal crisis such as: syncope/fainting, severe hypotension or shock, persistent nausea/vomiting or abdominal pain, and fever — these require emergency IV hydrocortisone and fluids, not outpatient follow-up.
management_principles: Plan for Addison Disease: Oral Hydrocortisone and Fludrocortisone, check baseline cortisol
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Autoimmune adrenal destruction causing fatigue, skin darkening, and low blood pressure on standing.
red_flags: Persistent nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain with fever — may herald adrenal (Addisonian) crisis and needs emergency IV hydrocortisone and fluids

must_ask.say: Do you feel dizzy standing up?

history.answer: I've been feeling completely exhausted lately, and people keep asking why my skin has turned so dark.
It feels like complete whole-body exhaustion and weakness, not just feeling sleepy.
It began about two months ago and has been steadily getting worse each week.
I can barely finish my workday, and even sleeping all weekend does not refresh me at all.
I feel tired all day long from the moment I wake up, and it gets even worse by the late afternoon.
I sleep around seven to eight hours every night without waking up, and my wife says I don't snore.
I feel frustrated about having no energy, but I'm not feeling depressed and I have no thoughts of self-harm.
I feel dizzy when I stand up, but I haven't had trouble breathing or noticed any black or bloody stools.
No, I haven't noticed easy bruising or bleeding from my gums.
No, I don't have any numbness, tingling, or pins and needles in my hands or feet.
I haven't been unusually sensitive to the cold, and my bowel movements have been regular with no constipation.
No, I haven't been excessively thirsty or needing to urinate more often than usual.
My skin looks like I've been tanning in the sun, especially on my hands, knuckles, and even inside my mouth.
Every time I stand up quickly from my chair or bed, my vision goes dark and I feel like I might faint.
My appetite has dropped, and I have unintentionally lost about five kilograms over the past two months.
Yes, strangely enough, I find myself craving salty snacks like potato chips and pickles all the time.
No, I haven't had any fevers, chills, or waking up drenched in sweat.
No shortness of breath when walking, and my legs and ankles haven't been swollen.
I have had mild nausea from time to time, but no severe abdominal cramps or vomiting.
I haven't actually blacked out or lost consciousness, though I have to sit down immediately when I get dizzy.
My workload is normal and I haven't had any unusual stress at work or at home.
I figured the dark skin and lightheadedness when I stand were just from severe dehydration and working too much in the sun.
I'm terrified I'm going to black out while driving my kids to school in the morning.
I'm hoping to get some fluids or a medication today to keep my blood pressure steady so I stop feeling faint.
I have always been healthy and have no history of high blood pressure, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any prescription drugs, over-the-counter pain relievers, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I drink maybe one beer once or twice a month socially, and I have one cup of coffee in the morning.
I work as an office manager at a logistics company and live with my wife.
My mother had an underactive thyroid, but no one in my family has had adrenal problems or other serious illnesses.

exam.finding: Patient appears fatigued and thin, with diffusely bronzed skin.
Blood pressure 104/66 mmHg, heart rate 86 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C.
Blood pressure drops to 84/54 mmHg upon standing, with heart rate increasing to 104 beats/min and mild lightheadedness.
Conjunctivae are slightly pale; sclerae are anicteric.
No palpable cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, with no palpable nodules.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or rubs.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, with no tenderness, guarding, or organomegaly.
No pretibial or ankle edema noted bilaterally.
Noticeable diffuse hyperpigmentation, prominent over knuckles, palmar creases, and dark bluish patches on the buccal mucosa.
